newsitem.title: USA: Union strikes GM wiring harness plants in Ohio.
newsitem.headline: Union strikes GM wiring harness plants in Ohio.

text.p: General Motors Corp.'s labor troubles escalated into a third strike early on Tuesday as more than 8,200 workers walked off the job at the automaker's electrical wiring harness factories in Warren, Ohio.
The strike could force GM, already battling walkouts at assembly plants in Michigan and Oklahoma, to shut down much of its North American operations if it drags on for a lenghty period.

The Delphi Packard Electric Systems plants produce wiring harnesses and wiring harness components used in most of GM's North American-built cars and trucks. The harnesses deliver electrical power and signals throughout the vehicle.
Workers walked out of the 16 Delphi Packard plants in the northeastern Ohio city after a 12:01 a.m. EST (0400 GMT) strike deadline expired without an agreement.

Local 717 President Nick Border said the main sticking points in the local contract negotiations revolve around job security -- the same as at many other GM parts and assembly plants that have run into labor disputes.
"We're trying to keep all of our people working so they have a place to retire from," Border said early on Tuesday.
GM has moved a significant amount of wiring harness assembly work to Mexico in recent years because it is highly labor intensive, requiring workers to wrap hundreds of wires together by hand.

Other demands by the union include abolishing the bottom tier of the plants' three-tier wage scale. Bottom-tier workers make 55 percent of the top-tier full wage. Local 717 members rejected a tentative pact in March, in part because it did not alter the tiered wage scale.

Deborah Ayers, a spokeswoman for GM's Delphi Packard Electric Systems division, said talks continued late on Monday night right up to the deadline before they broke off. She said it was not clear when they would resume.

GM has been hit with a rash of strikes in the past year over local labor contracts at individual plants, but this marks the first time in years that the automaker has simultaneously battled major strikes involving two different unions.
Workers represented by the United Auto Workers union struck GM's Oklahoma City car plant on April 4, while UAW members walked off the job at the company's Pontiac, Mich., truck plant on April 22.

In both of those strikes, the UAW is demanding that GM restore many jobs lost to attrition and efficiencies associated with new products. GM has resisted, saying it needs to shrink its workforce through natural attrition to become competitive.

The Pontiac plant is one of three North American factories that produce GM's full-size Chevrolet and GMC pickup trucks, while the Oklahoma City plant builds the Chevrolet Malibu and Oldsmobile mid-size sedans.
